summary: A checkpoint copies committed frames from the -wal file back into the main database file. SQLite runs a PASSIVE checkpoint automatically when a commit leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more. Manual modes (PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE) trade blocking for completeness. Checkpointing alone does not shrink the WAL file; the writer later rewinds and overwrites it, and only journal_size_limit or TRUNCATE shrink it on disk. A long-running reader can block completion and make the WAL grow without bound (checkpoint starvation). Checkpoint races also featured in a long-standing WAL-reset bug, fixed in 3.51.3. This matters for disk usage, read/write latency, and replication tools such as Litestream.

claims.text: By default SQLite runs an automatic checkpoint when a COMMIT leaves the WAL at 1000 pages or more (about 4MB), or when the last connection to the database closes. SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT changes the default.

Automatic checkpoints and sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() are PASSIVE: they copy as many frames as possible without taking locks that block others, never invoke the busy handler, and may not finish if readers or writers are active.

sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 has modes PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE (plus NOOP). FULL waits for no writer and all readers on the latest snapshot, blocking new writers. RESTART additionally waits until readers use only the database file so the next writer restarts the log. TRUNCATE does the same and truncates the WAL to zero bytes before returning.

If the busy handler returns 0 while a FULL/RESTART/TRUNCATE checkpoint waits for the writer lock or readers, the call falls back to PASSIVE behaviour and returns SQLITE_BUSY. If another process holds the checkpoint lock, it returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.

A checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless journal_size_limit is set). It lets SQLite overwrite the WAL from the start: a writer rewinds the WAL only when all frames are in the database, synced, and no reader uses the WAL. The -wal file keeps its high-water size on disk.

Checkpoint starvation: if there is always at least one active reader, no checkpoint can complete and the WAL grows without bound. SQLite's mitigations are reader gaps, or manual RESTART/TRUNCATE checkpoints, at the cost that readers may block while it runs.

Litestream runs PASSIVE checkpoints at 1000 pages or on a 1-minute interval, and forces a blocking TRUNCATE only past an emergency threshold (truncate-page-n, default 121,359 pages, ~500MB) after PASSIVE fails to bring the WAL below it. Forced TRUNCATE waits for readers and can stall writers; setting the threshold to 0 allows unbounded WAL growth.

Since SQLite 3.11.0 (2016-02-15) the WAL size for a single transaction is proportional to the transaction size; for transactions over about a gigabyte WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error.

A WAL-reset bug, present from 3.7.0 (2010) through 3.51.2, could mark WAL frames as checkpointed when they were not, so committed data could be lost when the WAL reset. It needs two or more connections writing or checkpointing at the same instant. It is fixed in 3.51.3 (2026-03-13), with backports 3.44.6 and 3.50.7. SQLite calls the real-world rate very low and says it is not an emergency.

sources.title: Another look at SQLite's WAL-Reset bug

disagreements.text: The SQLite page says the WAL-reset bug is fixed in 3.51.3 (backports 3.44.6, 3.50.7); the blog reports the fix as 3.53.0 and says it tested that build. The SQLite page is authoritative; the blog may name the first release it tested.
The SQLite WAL page lists only PASSIVE, FULL and RESTART as checkpoint subtypes in section 3.2 but mentions TRUNCATE elsewhere; the C API page lists all four.
